strengths: Substantially larger and more diverse dataset (1,048 scenes, 128 distractor types, 161 themes) than existing distractor-free benchmarks (RobustNeRF: 5 scenes, On-the-go: 12 scenes), addressing a genuine gap in the field with a well-documented, multi-month manual capture and curation pipeline (scene design, controllable/non-controllable capture, COLMAP pose estimation, instant-ngp verification, manual annotation).

The curated DF3DV-41 subset with 17 systematically designed distractor/scene scenarios (e.g., semantically similar, fluid, nighttime) provides fine-grained diagnostic value beyond aggregate scores, and the qualitative 'zoom-in no more' comparisons convincingly show the benchmark exposes larger, more visible performance gaps than prior saturated benchmarks.

Comprehensive benchmarking of 10 recent methods across four datasets (RobustNeRF, On-the-go, DF3DV-1K, DF3DV-41) with consistent methodology, producing an informative robustness ranking (AsymGS, RobustSplat as most robust) that appears to correlate sensibly with publication timeline, lending some external validity to the benchmark's difficulty calibration.

The DI2FIX application (fine-tuning DIFIX on DF3DV-1K) is a useful demonstration of the dataset's utility beyond static benchmarking, showing consistent gains across all evaluated methods and providing thorough ablations on training data scale and LPIPS-based pair filtering, plus an out-of-distribution generalization test.

Dataset difficulty is empirically justified via per-image performance distributions (Fig. 5) showing DF3DV-1K is harder than prior benchmarks under a common backbone (3DGS), which is a good sanity check rather than relying solely on scale claims.
weaknesses: The dataset itself does not appear to be released or verifiable at submission time (no explicit statement of a public release plan, license, or access instructions), which is a significant limitation for a datasets/benchmarks contribution whose core value depends on reproducibility and community adoption.

No discussion of privacy/ethical considerations despite outdoor scenes captured over 9 months likely containing passers-by, license plates, or other identifiable content (as referenced in distractor categories like 'common distractors as static parts: e.g., passer-by'); this is a meaningful omission for a large real-world capture dataset intended for public release.

Indoor distractors are manually introduced by operators per a predefined design, which may not perfectly reflect naturalistic 'casual capture' distractor distributions and could introduce systematic biases (e.g., overrepresentation of curated object types) relative to organically occurring clutter.

Evaluation relies solely on standard 2D image metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS); no human perceptual study or distractor-specific segmentation-based metric is used to validate that these metrics faithfully capture 'distractor removal quality' versus general reconstruction fidelity, despite the paper's core claim of being a distractor-focused benchmark.

The DI2FIX contribution is a relatively straightforward adaptation of an existing method (DIFIX) with a single component swap (reference view), and the reported improvements (0.96 dB PSNR, 0.057 LPIPS) are modest; this part reads more as an illustrative pilot study than a fully developed methodological contribution, which is appropriate as a secondary demonstration but should not be overweighted as a core contribution.

Some cited references have publication dates in 2026 (e.g., ICLR 2026, CVPR 2026, several arXiv entries dated late 2025/2026) which raises minor concerns about consistency of the timeline narrative and verifiability of comparisons to 'not yet published' concurrent datasets (RealX3D, T-3DGS, D-RE10K-iPhone) that could not be independently checked by reviewers.

Capture heterogeneity across 12 different consumer devices, 9 different resolutions, and multiple operators over 9 months, while framed as a diversity strength, could also introduce confounds (e.g., varying image quality, calibration consistency) that are not analyzed for their effect on benchmark reliability.

strengths: Significant scale increase over existing distractor-free NVS datasets (1,048 scenes vs. 5 for RobustNeRF and 12 for On-the-go), with both clean and cluttered image sets per scene, which is the key missing resource identified by the authors.

Systematic scenario design: 128 distractor types and 161 themes, plus a curated DF3DV-41 subset spanning 17 carefully designed distractor/scene scenarios, enabling fine-grained robustness analysis rather than only aggregate metrics.

Reasonably rigorous data curation pipeline (manual quality review, COLMAP pose estimation with joint clean/cluttered registration, instant-ngp sanity-check reconstruction, parameter re-tuning for failed scenes) that lends some credibility to data quality.

Comprehensive benchmarking of 9 recent distractor-free methods plus 3DGS, with consistent ranking trends across different splits (DF3DV-1K, DF3DV-41) that plausibly track publication timeline, lending some face validity to the benchmark.

The DI2FIX experiment is a useful demonstration of the dataset's downstream utility beyond pure benchmarking, including ablations on training-data scale and degradation-level thresholds and a leave-one-method-out generalization check.
weaknesses: Reproducibility/release status is unclear: the manuscript does not explicitly state dataset license terms or confirm public release, which is a critical requirement for a dataset-type contribution; without it, the central claimed contribution cannot be verified or used by the community.

For 'controllable' scenes, clean and cluttered images are captured in two separate passes; even with automatic exposure/focus, this introduces confounding nuisance variations (illumination, slight camera settings drift) between 'clean' and 'cluttered' sets that are not purely attributable to distractors, potentially biasing benchmark scores in ways not analyzed.

Average images per scene (~50-90 total, clean subset skewed toward fewer images) is comparatively sparse relative to other large-scale NVS datasets (e.g., DL3DV-10K), which may itself limit achievable reconstruction quality independent of distractors and confound the 'difficulty' narrative attributed solely to distractors.

Potential circularity in the DI2FIX evaluation: training pairs are generated by rendering the very benchmarked radiance-field methods on DF3DV-1K*, and while a leave-one-method-out test is included, the evaluation protocol and overlap between training/benchmark scene characteristics is not fully detailed, raising some concern about inflated improvement estimates.

No discussion of privacy/ethical considerations for a large-scale real-world capture dataset that likely includes identifiable people, private interiors, and locations, despite 9 months of consumer-camera data collection across many public/private scenes.

The benchmark protocol (hyperparameters, per-scene tuning or lack thereof, train/test view splits) is not described in sufficient detail to assess fairness across the nine compared methods, especially given the very large scene count makes exhaustive per-scene tuning unlikely.

The technical/algorithmic contribution (DI2FIX) is a relatively incremental fine-tuning of an existing 2D diffusion enhancer (DIFIX) rather than a novel method, and the reported gains (0.96 dB PSNR, 0.057 LPIPS) are modest relative to the scale of engineering effort invested in the dataset.

strengths: Substantially larger and more diverse than existing distractor-free NVS datasets (RobustNeRF, On-the-go): 1,048 scenes vs. 5-12, spanning 128 distractor types and 161 themes across both indoor and outdoor environments, with paired clean/cluttered images per scene captured over 9 months with consumer cameras.

The DF3DV-41 curated subset with 17 systematically designed distractor/scene scenarios (color-similar, semi-transparent, fluid, nighttime, etc.) is a thoughtful contribution that enables fine-grained diagnostic analysis beyond simple aggregate metrics, and reveals qualitatively visible failure modes without needing to zoom into subtle background regions, addressing a known saturation problem with prior benchmarks.

Comprehensive benchmarking of 10 recent methods (9 distractor-free methods + 3DGS) across four datasets (RobustNeRF, On-the-go, DF3DV-1K, DF3DV-41) provides a valuable, large-scale empirical comparison that is currently missing from the literature, and the finding that DF3DV-1K difficulty correlates with method publication timeline lends credibility to the benchmark's construction.

The data acquisition/curation pipeline (scene design, controllable vs. uncontrollable capture, COLMAP pose estimation with instant-ngp verification, manual metadata annotation) is clearly documented and appears methodologically sound for producing reliable ground-truth clean/cluttered pairs at scale.

The DI2FIX application is a nice value-add demonstrating a concrete downstream use of the dataset beyond passive benchmarking, with reasonable ablations on training data scale and LPIPS-based pair filtering threshold, plus an out-of-distribution (leave-one-method-out) generalization check.

Honest and specific discussion of limitations (dataset still smaller than general-purpose NVS datasets, residual cloud motion in "clean" images, DI2FIX failure modes/confirmation bias) rather than generic boilerplate.
weaknesses: Since this is fundamentally a dataset/benchmark paper, the core contribution's value hinges on data quality and correctness of ground truth (clean/cluttered alignment, pose accuracy) but the paper offers only qualitative/pipeline-level assurances (manual review by "two experts", instant-ngp verification) rather than quantitative measures of pose accuracy, annotation consistency/inter-annotator agreement, or residual distractor leakage rate in the "clean" sets.

The claim of 128 distractor types and 161 themes is a headline diversity number, but the distribution across these categories (e.g., how many scenes per type) is not shown in the main text (deferred to supplementary Fig. S.16), making it hard to judge whether the taxonomy is meaningfully populated or long-tailed/sparse in most categories.

The DI2FIX section, while a nice bonus, is a fairly thin technical contribution (essentially fine-tuning an existing method, DIFIX, by swapping the reference view) and the improvement magnitude (0.96 dB PSNR, 0.057 LPIPS) is evaluated only on a small held-out set (DF3DV-41, 41 scenes) plus On-the-go (12 scenes), limiting the statistical robustness of this secondary claim.

No dataset license, licensing/privacy considerations (e.g., captured people/faces/private property in casual outdoor/indoor scenes), or release/maintenance plan is discussed, which is an important consideration for large real-world capture datasets intended for public release.

The comparison table (Table 2) mixes released, unreleased, and "not published yet" datasets somewhat asymmetrically, and some claimed superiority (e.g., over concurrent works RealX3D and D-RE10K-iPhone) cannot be independently verified since those datasets are inaccessible, weakening the strength of relative positioning claims.

The paper's within-paper self-comparisons (e.g., method ranking following publication timeline) are interesting but could partly reflect that later methods were tuned/evaluated on datasets similar in spirit to On-the-go, and the paper does not fully rule out that its own benchmark still has biases favoring certain design choices (e.g., segmentation/semantic-feature reliance) discussed only qualitatively.
